method: Active uncertainty inventory regenerated after the two-pass audit of the historical register. Only included native phases with a last-confirmed endpoint are eligible; native reopening bounds and excluded phases do not carry old uncertainty forward. Matching historical resolutions are retained after scope reconciliation. Explicit later-access metadata may supply a qualified matching end bound; partial and exceptional access does not resolve unrelated traffic or crossings. The earlier review remains dated history. Separately sourced status observations and their supported timelines retain their actual check dates and do not alter historical duration totals.

records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

CC028-R1: HRW describes sporadic Armenia-directed transport interruptions from 1989 and a full blockade by summer 1991. June–August bounds represent the reported season, not a first day for each road or railway.

CC028-AUDIT20261026-1: HRW separately dates Nakhchivan’s blockade from June 1992. The parties disputed responsibility, and the source also describes earlier train attacks; those attacks are not treated as the same continuous blockade. June bounds preserve month precision.

Both restrictions were sustained and exceed 24 hours. Their chronology must not be combined into one common 1991 onset or one exact network-wide duration. Reuters described the heavily militarised interstate border as closed on 12 June 2025; FCDO advice checked 26 October 2026 still describes closure. These general confirmations do not enumerate each route or its exceptional movements.

Armenia’s prime minister stated on 11 March 2026 that rail shipments had arrived via Azerbaijan and Georgia from November 2025, while direct regional connections remained under development. Third-country transit is not direct Armenia–Azerbaijan border reopening.

Historical later-status finding retained where still applicable: Current advice explicitly says Armenia border remains closed; excludes exceptional and humanitarian passage.

records.title: Turkey–Armenia longstanding land-border closure
records.check_kind: Ledger reconciliation after two full source audits; not a new source-observation date
records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

CC004-D1: Official history places the closure in 1993 and Crisis Group in early April. Scholarly research by Vahram Ter-Matevosyan qualifies this: before April, crossings were already limited to agreed uses, including humanitarian transport and rail traffic. April 1993 is therefore a historical tightening milestone, not proof that an ordinary public border first closed then. No exact first onset or uninterrupted duration is assigned.

Authorised humanitarian crossings in February 2023 and a Syria-bound convoy entering on 22 March 2025 are exceptions. Türkiye also identifies reciprocal diplomatic pedestrian crossings on 30 July 2024 and routine border-commission use. These do not establish ordinary reopening.

The 13 May 2026 Turkish statement concerns trade documentation via third countries and says work on opening the common border is ongoing. FCDO advice checked 26 October 2026 still describes the land border as closed; this is current advisory evidence, not a newly dated operational observation at every post.

Separately dated later evidence: 2024-07-30: Authorised reciprocal diplomatic pedestrian crossings; not ordinary public travel. This evidence does not resolve the whole phase. 2025-03-22: Authorised Syria-bound humanitarian convoy entry; not ordinary public travel. This evidence does not resolve the whole phase.

Historical later-status finding retained where still applicable: Current FCDO guidance still excludes ordinary direct Armenia–Turkey land travel; authorised humanitarian exceptions do not constitute general reopening.

phases.scope: Ordinary direct land travel across the Turkey–Armenia frontier is unavailable, with individually authorised exceptions.

records.title: Azerbaijan prolonged pandemic land-entry closure
records.check_kind: Ledger reconciliation after two full source audits; not a new source-observation date
records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: qualified. The narrow road-entry scope survives review; current advice still overgeneralizes rail and exit rules, so specific Azerbaijani permissions remain essential.

Mainland restrictions began in stages: Iran February 29, Georgia March 14 and Russia March 18, 2020. No simultaneous national onset is implied. Uniform exit rules remain outside the retained road-entry scope. September 3, 2026 is a dated last confirmation, not an assumed cutoff or future extension.

CC003-D1: Nakhchivan–Turkey phases and Georgia passenger rail reopening are excluded. The September Czech page's all-land wording conflicts with Azerbaijan's specific rail permission from 25 May 2026 and documented 26 May outward train. Exit rules differ; no post-3 September persistence inferred.

Historical later-status finding retained where still applicable: Ordinary foreign road entry still requires special permission. Official MFA allows foreign land exit without permission and eligible Georgia rail entry; conflicting blanket advisory wording is not adopted.

phases.scope: Ordinary non-permitted foreign road entry into mainland Azerbaijan across the Georgia, Russia and Iran frontiers; freight and individually authorised entry excluded.

records.check_kind: Ledger reconciliation after two full source audits; not a new source-observation date
records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

CC020-D1: An envelope of protest obstruction, checkpoint control and tightening aid restrictions. Medical and family passage occurred, and ordinary passage in May/June was contested. August 18 is a last confirmation, not a reopening. Envelope length is not days fully closed.

ICRC directly records aid delivery through Lachin on 18 September 2023. On 24 September, EFE reported the first group of refugees arriving in Armenia through the corridor with Russian peacekeeper accompaniment. These are different scoped access observations: aid entry and outward refugee passage. They do not establish a first ordinary two-way reopening, uninterrupted access thereafter, or continued closure to the present.

Separately dated later evidence: 2023-09-18: ICRC aid delivery through Lachin; not ordinary two-way passage. This evidence does not resolve the whole phase. 2023-09-24: Refugee arrivals in Armenia through Lachin; not ordinary two-way passage. This evidence does not resolve the whole phase.

phases.scope: Phased restriction of ordinary and humanitarian access along Lachin from the December protest obstruction through the August aid-access crisis; movement classes and mechanisms changed.

records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: qualified. Fresh operator notices confirm the March 5 Rason suspension, June 16 ordinary-tourism non-reopening and separately dated October 2026 status. Exceptions and unresolved rationale are correctly retained.

EA024-D1: Both operators may relay the same instruction. Industry/staff visits and tourism elsewhere are not ordinary Rason land tours. The earlier evidence segment ends on June 16, 2025; a separate operator observation dated October 1, 2026 supplies the later status below. Other traveller classes are not covered.

rationale: The direct tour operator’s dated notices still provide no reason. Do not inherit the 2020 COVID rationale or infer motives from later business exceptions.

Later observation: Young Pioneer Tours, updated October 1, 2026, reports that ordinary non-Russian tourism remains suspended, linking this to the March 5, 2025 reversal. Historical later-status finding retained where still applicable: Operating tour agencies report ordinary non-Russian tourism still suspended, including Rason; Russian and special-delegation exceptions must be retained.

records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: qualified. Fresh official and contemporary sources confirm the existing distinction between June 8 selective restrictions and June 23 command orders. Humanitarian exceptions and later current closure advice do not establish uniform historical enforcement.

EA001-FU1: Formal restriction confirmed on June 23 only. Later exceptions and uneven changes require separately matched phases; no uninterrupted whole-frontier operation or present closure inferred.

REC50-R28-PH001: The narrow rule is confirmed on 8 June; no exact effective time, first refusal, end or intervening continuity is supplied. Larger trucks can use the alternative Friendship Bridge checkpoint. The later June 23 command orders remain a separate existing phase. The official stated purpose here is peace, order and safety; the parent’s crime rationale is not automatically attributed to this early phase.

duration: The dated formal restriction can be represented as confirmed at June 23. Full-regime endpoint and operational continuity remain unresolved.

Historical later-status finding retained where still applicable: Current traveller advice reports Thai–Cambodian land crossings closed. Retain the separate historical tourism restriction rather than infer its exact endpoint.

records.title: Cambodian goods and passenger restrictions at the Thailand frontier during border disputes
records.check_kind: Ledger reconciliation after two full source audits; not a new source-observation date
records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

EA002-FU1: The national general-goods prohibition is confirmed on June 29, 2025; its original onset and repeal remain unknown. Nationwide physical enforcement is not independently observed. A June 24 Poipet return arrangement supplies an earlier, geographically limited goods prohibition, but does not establish a national start date. Its scheduled passenger-return hours do not prove actual passage throughout the window.

EA002-R2-P1: Customs and immigration officials confirmed the narrower Thai fruit-and-vegetable restriction on June 17, 2025, with the immigration director reporting a 09:00 start. Other goods and passengers remained permitted in that account. The exact ending and continuous gate-level enforcement of this commodity measure remain unestablished.

EA002-AUDIT20261025-1: The December 13, 2025 suspension of all entry and exit is a distinct formal scope, effective immediately according to the Ministry of Interior. It does not backdate the goods prohibitions. The June 13, 2026 statement is a separate later goods-policy observation that distinguishes sea and air channels. No uninterrupted all-crossing operation or all-person continuity is inferred.

Separately dated later evidence: 2025-06-24: Poipet goods prohibition during specified return arrangements; not national onset This evidence does not resolve the whole phase. 2026-06-13: Land-border goods imports into Cambodia remained prohibited; sea and air distinguished This evidence does not resolve the whole phase.

records.title: Brunei land border COVID restrictions
records.check_kind: Ledger reconciliation after two full source audits; not a new source-observation date
records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: qualified. The initial foreign-entry ban, later approved-entry categories, selected 2022 extensions and August 1 Sungai Tujoh access are supported without a uniform multi-year closure claim.

EA019-R1: ASEAN February 14 report inspected fully and explicitly calls this a fourteen-day scheduled extension. The 13-day date subtraction is an endpoint difference, not the number of listed calendar dates or elapsed closure hours. Includes foreign land-entry/transit and work-commuter movements with approved exceptions. No February 28 observed reopening.

EA019-R2: Scheduled restriction window from June 15 through July 31; official consular notice anticipates conditional August 1 easing. The 46-day endpoint subtraction is not a claim of 46 or 47 elapsed closed days. Actual operation at every crossing/direction and intervening policy chain remain unestablished.

EA019-C7P1: Institutional indexed chronology; original February 26 release not recovered. Scheduled window only; actual enforcement and expiry not observed. Do not bridge all earlier/later periods into continuous closure.

EA019-C7P2: Original PDF currently returns 404; indexed official text and AMRO chronology agree. This is an announced extension, not observed gate continuity or March 31 reopening.

The March 24, 2020 initial foreign-entry/transit prohibition is separately documented by the Philippine government. August 1, 2022 field reporting observes ordinary travellers at Sungai Tujoh, converting that gate’s earlier reopening plan into a later-access observation. The full intervening policy chain and other crossings remain qualified.

phases.scope: Brunei foreign-national entry and transit prohibition, including land admission.

records.title: Hungary first pandemic foreigner-entry prohibition
records.check_kind: Ledger reconciliation after two full source audits; not a new source-observation date
records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

March 17, 2020 is the formal onset of the general foreign-entry restriction, with citizen return and discretionary exceptions. Changing commuter/resident exceptions and bilateral easing preclude an unchanged March-to-June closure. June 5 permits Austrian, Czech and Slovak citizens unrestricted entry. The June 18 Hungarian embassy notice and Decree 291/2020 now establish broader EU/EEA/Swiss and qualifying family access, with UK citizens excluded from that category and separate Serbian permission. Ukrainian citizens had a limited 24-hour, 30-kilometre border-area permission, not unrestricted national access. Other foreigners generally still required police permission. These are scoped policy changes, not actual first crossings or universal reopening. The legal register displays the July 4 consolidated text; the contemporaneous embassy notice independently identifies the June 18 categories.

Historical later-status finding retained where still applicable: Police explicitly confirm entry by road regardless of citizenship or coronavirus protection; earlier intermediate reopening dates not inferred.

phases.scope: Hungarian land entry under initial nationwide regime

The two named posts closed August 18, 2023. An October 30, 2025 retrospective and the official checkpoint directory inspected in October 2026 retain their closed status; the latter is current standing directory information, not a daily operational history. Light vehicles used both posts and empty freight trucks also used Tverečius. The other four crossings remained available at onset. Exceptional permissions are not comprehensively enumerated.

Historical later-status finding retained where still applicable: The official checkpoint directory updated 1 October 2026 explicitly lists both Šumskas and Tverečius as temporarily closed. Together with the operative 18 August 2023 closure and the historical October 2025 confirmation, this supports the continuing named-post regime. It is not a closure of the entire Lithuania–Belarus frontier.

EU007-C7P1: The government decision announced on 19 November 2025 retained vehicle-only passage when Medininkai and Šalčininkai reopened from 20 November. Historical later-status finding retained where still applicable: The official checkpoint directory updated 1 October 2026 explicitly lists Lavoriškės and Raigardas as temporarily closed. The road-post closure is supported from its 1 March 2024 effective date. The separately coded pedestrian/cycle and railway boarding phases retain their unresolved later status; this road-post evidence does not resolve them.

records.title: Rwanda restriction at Gatuna and on travel to Uganda
records.check_kind: Ledger reconciliation after two full source audits; not a new source-observation date
records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

Passenger denial is reported for February 28, 2019 and directly observed on March 1; exact first onset remains unresolved. Dated denials and selective permissions do not establish a continuous 2019–2022 all-traffic closure. Preserve February 28 freight diversion, June 10–22 truck trial, January 31, 2022 cargo/returnee permission, March 7 outgoing bus and later local-shopping relaxation as different scopes. Freight eligibility remains contested; national COVID policy is GL04.

GL01-R1: Formal heavy-truck diversion effective February 28 until June 10 trial permission. RRA officially cited construction; Ugandan officials disputed this and alleged broader passenger denials. Eligibility of a construction-only diversion is not independently established; record remains eligible for documented coercive movement restrictions. Alternative routes remained available; no actual first-trial passage time established.

GL01-R2: Observed June 23 around 01:00 reclosure; January 31 2022 cargo resumption only. URN quotes an unnamed officer citing structural cracks, while reporting broader political allegations and travel restrictions. Political character is contested for the narrowly scoped freight measure; continuity relies on retrospective reporting and overlaps pandemic rules.

GL01-C7RWP1: The EastAfrican March 1 report describes the previous Thursday, February 28, when a Gatuna bus was allowed through after its Rwandan passengers and driver were refused; it also directly observes nationality-selective access on March 1. Neither is necessarily the first onset. Ugandan official accounts indicate earlier restrictions; Kigali officials described an advisory and denied a general closure. Construction claims do not erase the separate passenger evidence.

GL01-C7RWP2: Further dated confirmation, not proof of uninterrupted enforcement since March. August ministerial statement supports continuing advisory language, not universal denial.

GL01-C7RWP3: Last-confirmed is report date, not first relaxation. Roughly two-month retrospective description is not converted to an exact onset. Detailed anonymous interview concerns Kagitumba; introduction names Gatuna. One outlet does not establish uniform gate practice.

GL01-C7RWP4: Date-specific observation; no continuity from 2019 inferred. Cargo, Rwandan citizens and returning residents could enter Rwanda. National COVID policy is GL04; exact political/health overlap unresolved.

GL01-C7RWP5: No reverse passenger vehicle observed by the report’s 17:00 cutoff. Some passengers could not meet testing costs. National permission and this passage do not establish all-gate/group normalization; Cyanika ID travel remained restricted. Onset and continuous duration unknown.

GL01-C7RWP6: Calendar normalization of a dated relative reference, not a retrieved order. Local shopping differs from earlier passenger permission; food limits and changed testing remain. Do not extrapolate to every gate, traveler or commodity; onset and duration unknown.

phase eligibility/motive: Narrow freight-diversion phases have explicit construction/safety explanations as well as disputed political context.

onset: Passenger denial is reported for February 28 and directly observed on March 1, 2019. Earlier Ugandan official reports and the World Bank retrospective March 6 date do not establish a single first day for every gate or traffic class.

continuity: The observations do not establish one uninterrupted 2019–2022 passenger prohibition. Selective permissions existed before COVID; GL04 separately records the overlapping national health policy.

Historical later-status finding retained where still applicable: Observed Rwandan passenger and ordinary trader access resumed in stages; March 7 bus access alone did not end every cohort restriction.

phases.scope: Observed denial of Rwandan passenger exit at Gatuna; foreign travelers remained able to cross
Rwandan travel toward Uganda still restricted at Gatuna despite June truck trial
Selective permission and refusal for Rwandan travel to Uganda, reported at Kagitumba and Gatuna
Ordinary passenger denials at Gatuna during cargo/returnee reopening

records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

GL16-R1 concerns entry into Burundi, including Congolese transit passengers. The March onset is supported, but a universal uninterrupted March 2020–October 2022 operational interval is not established. September 2020 authorised returns at Gasenyi–Nemba and September 2022 Mapassa passage at Ruhwa are narrower exceptions or access observations, not dates of general passenger reopening. The latter supplies matching-direction evidence absent from the September 30 outward-passage report. Political and health restrictions overlap. The reported long wait of the September 2020 returnees establishes a restriction exceeding 24 hours for that cohort, without fixing every traveller’s duration, the Ruhwa endpoint or the precise repeal of the original health measure. Cargo evidence remains separate.

Scope reconciliation: Final audit distinguishes Mapassa-cohort inward access, September 30 outward movement and October 22 formal reopening from ordinary Ruhwa entry and repeal of the health rule. Preserve partial evidence without applying the old whole-phase access bound.

Separately dated later evidence: 2022-09-06: Mapassa agency clients entering Burundi at Ruhwa, including Congolese and Burundian passengers. This evidence does not resolve the whole phase.

phases.scope: Ruhwa refusal of entry into Burundi from Rwanda.

records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

GL12-FU1: The June 20, 2022 order prohibits goods imports and exports through Bunagana. M23 announced physical reopening the same day; journalists subsequently observed trade under its appointed administration in the week reported on April 21, 2023. These are evidence of traffic despite the Congolese prohibition, not its legal repeal. The July 5, 2023 letter envisaged a conditional return of Congolese state services, not a completed reopening, and M23 opposed that return. Uganda’s July 10, 2025 reopening likewise does not establish repeal by the DRC. The prohibition’s legal endpoint and continuity remain unknown; no uninterrupted operational closure or numeric duration is inferred.

phases.scope: Bunagana goods import/export prohibition by North Kivu authorities

records.title: DRC election border closure extending beyond announced day at Mpondwe
records.check_kind: Ledger reconciliation after two full source audits; not a new source-observation date
records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: qualified. Fresh source inspection supports the scoped election closure and voter exception. No earlier matched reopening was found; the later Kasindi trade resumption belongs to a separate strike and cannot supply an exact election-closure endpoint.

GL10-D1: Onset remains December 19–20, 2023. The national December 20 00:00–23:59 schedule was not actual local reopening: Mpondwe still prevented entry/exit at 15:00 on December 21. The first subsequent reopening is unknown.

A separate December 20 Election-net report says Congolese arriving from Burundi and Rwanda crossed at Ruzizi around 11:00 to vote. This is an incoming voting exception, not general border restoration; the report does not identify each bridge. It qualifies broad claims that every Rwanda-frontier traveller was excluded.

Le Quotidien RDC reports actual import/export resumption at Kasindi late on June 18, 2024, with resident testimony, following a separate seven-day strike. Fish-sector disruption continued. This is a later scoped freight-access observation only: do not extend the election closure continuously to June, assign all passengers the freight endpoint or merge the unrelated strike into this episode.

Separately dated later evidence: 2024-06-18: Kasindi import/export freight after a separate strike; fish-sector and general passenger access are not resolved. This evidence does not resolve the whole phase.

phases.scope: Mpondwe–Kasindi election interruption, confirmed still closed at 15:00 on December 21.

records.title: Uganda closure of Bunagana and Ishasha adjoining M23-held territory
records.check_kind: Ledger reconciliation after two full source audits; not a new source-observation date
records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

GL13-D1: The exact late-January onset is unknown; the whole-month range does not assert January 1. July 10 is officially reported reactivation at Bunagana and Ishasha, including a Bunagana ceremony, not independently established first ordinary passage at both posts. Informal Bunagana movement continued. August 4 reporting confirms small-truck local trade while heavy international traffic remained limited; its retrospective since-2021 wording is not used to replace this phase’s January 2025 onset.

GL13-R1: Busanza’s July 9 endpoint is presidential permission, not verified first ordinary passage. Its unknown January onset and policy duration remain separate from the other posts; no continuous physical seal is inferred.

REC50-R26-GL13-P1: URN’s March 5 account names four routes to Goma, but the fuller March 3 memo quotation in Monitor and New Vision’s account name six posts and DRC-bound goods, including Bukavu. The original attachment requires client access and was not inspected. The stated aim was preventing revenue loss after DRC authorities lost control of Goma and Bukavu; goods were directed to alternative posts. Monitor’s March 11 and March 17 reports identify March 10 stranded trucks at Katuna and Cyanika; the later publication is not a new truck-observation date. The driver’s reported nine-day wait supports a sustained restriction for that cohort, not an exact onset at every post. No general passenger closure, universal all-goods ban, July repeal of this routing rule or exact first clearance restoration is inferred.

phases.scope: URA routing restriction on DRC-bound goods clearance through Katuna, Bunagana, Cyanika (Chanika), Ishasha, Busanza and Kyeshero; affected destinations include Goma and Bukavu.

records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

H03-D1: Reuters and The Reporter disagree over which crossing changed on December 26 versus 27, so those bounds are retained. Reuters describes Eritrean entry and Ethiopian exit as permitted; The Reporter describes broader trader return difficulties. An on-site journalist’s May 15, 2019 account reports business disruption since the reclosure at Zalambessa, supporting a sustained restriction beyond the original December evidence. This does not mean that all authorised or informal movement ceased. The page’s later 2024 update label is not the event date.

H03-R1: Rama’s permit requirement for Ethiopian citizens and Ethiopian-licensed vehicles retains the December 28 last confirmation; the May Zalambessa observation does not extend Rama. No exact first reopening is established.

On June 22, 2025, a community-led reunion at Zalambessa included travellers from Eritrea, and BBC reporting described resumed nearby cross-border trade. This was local access without formal bilateral reopening, after the separate 2020 war; it is not proof that the December 2018 Ethiopian-entry restriction lasted continuously until 2025 or ended on that day. An April 6, 2019 Ministry of Information commentary mentions legal arrangements for unspecified partially restricted areas, but supplies no named-gate order or dated rationale for these phases.

phases.scope: Ethiopian entry into Eritrea at Zalambessa–Serha, with a later May 15, 2019 account of sustained disruption to ordinary cross-border business.
Ethiopian citizens and Ethiopian-licensed vehicles entering Eritrea at Rama without newly required permits.

records.title: Kenya COVID passenger closure at Tanzania and Somalia borders
records.check_kind: Ledger reconciliation after two full source audits; not a new source-observation date
records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

H08-FU1: The overnight May 16–17 onset is retained. FEWS NET’s June assessment, reporting conditions through June 30, describes the government’s passenger prohibition at both Tanzania and Somalia borders as indefinite. Kenya News Agency’s June 12 report independently documents continued human-traffic closure at the Lunga Lunga–Horo Horo area, with interception of attempted informal crossings. This supports sustained restriction beyond the initial announcement without claiming an impermeable frontier.

Cargo vehicles remained exempt subject to driver testing. The May 22 agreement also allowed locally identified border farmers to reach their plots; its trade-reopening language is not a general passenger reopening. Neither the June 6 domestic-curfew date nor a scheduled 30-day period supplies an actual land-border endpoint.

The May 2022 EABC interview documents Riverside’s ordinary Namanga shuttle services during October 2021, including actual passenger loads. This is a later operator-specific access bound, not proof of continuous closure since May 2020, first border reopening, uniform access at other Tanzania posts, or any Somalia endpoint. A broad August customs summary of permitted Kenyan travel does not identify these land cohorts or a repeal instrument.

Separately dated later evidence: 2021-10-31: Riverside passenger shuttles via Namanga on the Nairobi–Arusha–Moshi route only. This evidence does not resolve the whole phase.

phases.scope: Kenya–Tanzania and Kenya–Somalia land borders as covered by the Kenyan order

records.title: Djibouti second COVID land passenger closure in October 2020
records.check_kind: Ledger reconciliation after two full source audits; not a new source-observation date
records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

H21-R1: The original decree is legally effective October 20, 2020 for fifteen days. November 3–4 are alternative counting interpretations of the stated duration, not independently observed gate reopening dates. The decree exempts goods but does not expressly exempt returning nationals.

H21-C7P1: La Nation’s October 22 account dates implementation to the previous Wednesday, October 21. The full IOM October monthly report retrospectively describes an imposed fifteen-day land restriction from October 20 that had little effect on monitored migrant flows. WHO’s January 3 review also describes the fifteen-day measure. This supports a sustained restriction longer than 24 hours, while the legal/implementation date difference and exact operational endpoint remain unresolved. It does not establish that every gate stopped all traffic.

The earlier returning-national exception remains attributed to the indexed regional IOM account, not to the decree. Irregular migration during the restriction does not establish ordinary passenger reopening.

Later status: newly recovered indexed Newland Chase guidance dated December 4, 2020 already describes air, land and sea borders as open under testing conditions; the December 10 bulletin repeats this. These are qualified later advisory-status observations, not an exact first gate reopening, legal repeal or operation at every post. A December 3 secondary tracker also reports reopening but its cited original advisory remains unrecovered. November advisory repetition of the original fifteen-day wording cannot independently establish continuing enforcement after the scheduled expiry.

Separately dated later evidence: 2020-12-04: Djibouti land-passenger access subject to testing. Matching whole-phase uncertainty is bounded; exact first reopening is not inferred.

Matching end bounds have been integrated from explicit phase-scoped audit metadata.

records.title: Eritrea COVID land-border closure overlay
records.check_kind: Ledger reconciliation after two full source audits; not a new source-observation date
records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

H20-NP1: The June 11, 2020 Eritrean foreign-ministry statement, published June 12, places border restrictions broadly after the first COVID case on March 21, without an exact land commencement. Neither the March 26 aviation date nor the April 2 domestic lockdown date is transferred to land crossings. Continuing land arrivals and quarantine are expressly acknowledged; this was not an impermeable physical seal.

COMESA’s November 13, 2020 compilation is a policy assessment reference, not an independently observed gate timestamp. The 2020 US human-rights report describes continuing closure to legal overland travel, without isolating COVID from inherited bilateral restrictions.

A WCO regional report describes the position as of August 2021: land and sea borders remained closed except screened cargo, with several COVID restrictions unchanged since June. Its Eritrea passage cites a GardaWorld August 12 bulletin. This supports a later reported passenger-policy restriction and a sustained restriction longer than 24 hours. It does not establish exact complete duration or an uninterrupted operational bridge from 2020. The WCO report’s October 26 publication is not the status date.

No terminal COVID-specific land reopening is established. Later Sudan humanitarian access or continuing Ethiopia/Djibouti bilateral closure cannot by themselves identify repeal of this overlay.

records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

NA012-C7P1 records an August 5, 2024 observation that Ghadames–Debdeb remained closed to citizen travel for security reasons on the Libyan side. LANA’s August 3, 2023 report also distinguishes passenger reopening preparations from existing commercial traffic. Anadolu identifies May 2014 as Ghadames–Debdeb’s historical closure, while its 2011 closure and 2015 local exceptions concern Tin Al Koum and Tarat; LANA’s broad frontier summary is less gate-specific. These historical accounts do not establish one continuous Ghadames passenger interval: a June 2020 contemporary report describes limited exceptional departures and stranded Libyans awaiting further permission. The planned December 12, 2023 reopening was expressly postponed. Indexed regional reporting dated August 5, 2026 still describes preparations with no announced reopening date, not observed gate-level passage. The repeated descriptions of an ordinary passenger restriction pending reopening in August and December 2023 and still closed in August 2024 support a restriction longer than 24 hours, independently of the unknown exact onset. Authorized exceptional departures do not contradict the non-exempt passenger restriction. First ordinary passenger restoration, exact onset of the present spell and continuous numeric duration remain unresolved.

records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

No uninterrupted March–August all-traffic closure is established. The existing March21 endpoint remains food/essential-goods freight only.

SA003-D1: The contemporary March 2 notice is preferred but the contrary day is not erased. Passenger return windows and later cargo schedules are separate; the initial planned March 9 expiry is not used.

SA003-C7P1: First start of this recurring arrangement is unknown. June20 announcement reiterates Saturday access but does not supply a later observed passenger-crossing day. Freight and exceptional returns are separate; do not infer continuous sealing.

SA003-C7P2: Anadolu reports officials confirming that passenger movement resumed on 21 August, alongside the seven-day operating agreement. This is evidence of restored operation by that date, although no individual first crossing or exact earlier easing is timed. Prior Saturday and exceptional openings preclude an uninterrupted March–August closure; the headline’s six-month shorthand does not override those documented openings.

Separately dated later evidence: 2020-08-21: Seven-day Chaman passenger access superseded the Saturday-only arrangement. Matching whole-phase uncertainty is bounded; exact first reopening is not inferred.

Matching end bounds have been integrated from explicit phase-scoped audit metadata.

phases.scope: Chaman pedestrian eligibility restricted to scheduled Saturday access, with health conditions

records.title: India national COVID land-passenger restrictions
records.check_kind: Ledger reconciliation after two full source audits; not a new source-observation date
records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

SA019-FU1: Censored formal policy phase, not continuous all-passenger operational closure. It is a later phase of the national policy, not the March 15/16 selected-post rule. No matched land reopening date inferred from eventual air resumption.

end: No matched repeal of the original selected-land-post restriction was found. Air and visa relaxations do not establish all-land reopening.

duration: A distinct subsequent March 23 incoming-passenger formal phase is evidenced through May 7, with exceptions; complete operational duration remains unavailable.

The 16 March 2022 tourist-visa restoration still excluded land entry on tourist visas. The Ministry of Home Affairs 2022–23 annual-report extract subsequently records 20 land immigration posts reopened, distributed across the Bangladesh, Bhutan, Nepal and Pakistan borders. It supplies neither a common reopening date nor a repeal for every land post, and does not include Myanmar in that reopened subset. These later, differently scoped measures must not be used to project the original all-land restriction indefinitely or to invent a single national endpoint.

phases.scope: Land immigration posts within the March 23 all-107-post incoming-passenger policy; non-land posts excluded from this phase

records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

SA025-D1 remains reference only and excluded from animation and numeric closure analysis. Contemporary road reports describe absent staff, voluntary nonacceptance of cargo and insecurity; they do not establish deliberate border denial. The road dates remain August 5–8, with some source wording differing over the time of cessation.

SA025-AUDIT20261026-1: This is a separate deliberate rail restriction, not a reason to include SA025-D1. UNB and the Daily Star report Benapole rail-goods restoration on September 4 and describe 47 days since July 19. However, the August 19 Daily Star report already records Indian Railways’ verbal decision for freight restoration the following day; a later New Age official account dates wider freight restoration to August 20, and the September 8 Times of India mentions rakes dispatched during the preceding two weeks. These are not fully reconciled at the Benapole gate level. September 4 is therefore retained as confirmed access by that date, not an uncontested first reopening. The confirmed pre-restoration span ends August 19; no uninterrupted closure is assumed afterwards. Passenger trains remained a distinct restriction and are not assigned the freight endpoint.

Separately dated later evidence: 2024-09-04: Goods trains operating through Petrapole–Benapole; exact first local freight return unresolved; passenger rail excluded. Matching whole-phase uncertainty is bounded; exact first reopening is not inferred.

Matching end bounds have been integrated from explicit phase-scoped audit metadata.

phases.scope: Cross-border rail freight through Petrapole–Benapole, within the India–Bangladesh rail suspension.

records.title: Liberia COVID land-border closure
records.check_kind: Ledger reconciliation after two full source audits; not a new source-observation date
records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

W-022-FU1: The contemporary report places Liberia’s Guinea and Côte d’Ivoire first-phase closure on 30 March 2020. It does not date the Sierra Leone phase or establish a continuous physical closure. Cargo transfers and humanitarian exceptions remained. A Liberia Revenue Authority statement dated 4 May describes the continuing passenger restrictions and cargo arrangements.

Ganta–Guinea later access: Local Voices Liberia’s report published 12 March 2021 quotes the Nimba immigration deputy commander saying the official border had reopened for travellers under health screening, alongside interviews with local traders. This supports official passenger access by that date at Ganta, not an exact first reopening day, observed first crossing, nationwide repeal or an endpoint for Côte d’Ivoire. The report also describes irregular passage during the closure.

An SSHAP March 2021 briefing reports an earlier Guinea–Liberia reopening in October 2020. The relevant passage was recovered from a transcription, but its underlying footnote and exact crossing/side could not be verified. It is not adopted as an exact endpoint or used to infer uninterrupted closure until March 2021.

IOM’s December 2021 survey describes increased movement after reopening across official and unofficial Sierra Leone border points. This is a different frontier and does not end the Guinea/Côte d’Ivoire phase. A secondary tracker’s 13 October 2021 full-land-reopening claim remains uncorroborated by the original dated FCDO advice. Other gates’ first passenger restoration and national formal repeal remain unknown; the old COVID restriction is not asserted to continue into the present.

Separately dated later evidence: 2020-05-04: Liberia Revenue Authority describes continuing national passenger restrictions and cargo exceptions; not a new gate onset This evidence does not resolve the whole phase. 2021-03-12: Ganta official passenger reopening reported; no Côte d’Ivoire or all-gate endpoint This evidence does not resolve the whole phase.

phases.scope: Liberia closure toward Guinea and Côte d’Ivoire, first phase

Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

March 17 selective restrictions and April 30 customs status are directly supported. The March 16, 2022 cabinet statement expressly describes land, air and sea entry subject to negative PCR or antigen tests, and exits subject to destination-country requirements. It no longer describes eligibility as limited to indispensable journeys. We therefore infer an earlier ended-by bound for the essential-only restriction from this general traveller regime. The statement does not explicitly name a repeal clause or identify the first ordinary passenger crossing.

June 16, 2022 removes later testing/document requirements; it should not prolong the earlier essential-travel closure interval. Neither observation proves continuous enforcement since March 2020. Cargo and indispensable-travel exceptions, and independent neighbouring-country restrictions, remain separate.

Separately dated later evidence: 2022-03-16: Inferred end of Benin essential-only traveller eligibility from cabinet description of general land entry with tests and departure subject to destination rules; not explicit repeal or first crossing. records.check_kind: Ledger reconciliation after two full source audits; not a new source-observation date
records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

The initial four-frontier rule began March 13, 2020; the Polish-frontier extension began March 17. Citizen, residence and freight exceptions remain. June 5 easing applies to the four participating countries’ citizens; June 20 easing concerns travel from Poland. A July 21, 2021 Ukrainian government news report records permission for fully vaccinated Ukrainian citizens. Its detailed foreign-ministry guidance limits unvaccinated admission to specified residence, family and student categories; it does not establish ordinary entry for all unvaccinated Ukrainians. July 21 is a later policy-permission observation, not the first operational crossing or proof that the original restriction continued unchanged until then. No universal endpoint for every foreign-nonresident cohort is established. The April 6, 2022 source repeals quarantine and registration while expressly preserving other entry conditions, so it is not alone a blanket admission-ban repeal.

Historical later-status finding retained where still applicable: Official sources state COVID entry regime no longer restricted; local temporary controls are separate.

records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

R2-AF-006-FU1: Contemporary AFP and Xinhua reports place the immediate order on Sunday March 3, 2019. The later VOA account says March 5 and even calls that date Sunday; this inconsistent retrospective wording does not displace the contemporary chronology. FEWS NET reports current border-closure supply effects in March and their continuation in April 2019. April is an assessment month, not an exact gate-observation date. This supports a sustained restriction exceeding 24 hours, while porous desert routes, unspecified category exemptions and later August corridor exceptions prevent a claim of complete sealing or uninterrupted March–August operation. The exact reopening remains unknown.

phases.scope: Chadian restriction on the Libya land frontier; subsequent supply impacts documented in Tibesti

records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

The UN later dates the announcement to August 21, while local Tuesday/date wording is inconsistent; no exact original effective day is imposed. September reporting and Crisis Group interviews describe continuing Libya- and Sudan-related supply restrictions with open designated corridors; this does not independently confirm every CAR route in September. Puerto Acosta's physical crossing conditions and exact customs-service resumption remain unverified. The official PDF could not be opened, but its operative text was recovered in the official search index.

Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

R3-AM-001-R2OBS1: January 4 is a contemporary observed renewed onset after the holiday truce, not an inferred start from a later report. It does not prove uninterrupted closure until March. Traveler eligibility differed by bridge and heavy-freight hours differed from passenger access. March 24 immigration-control resumption occurred on flexible days. June 23 CEBAF immigration-control resumption concerns a separate facility and does not establish the final end of the bridge-blockade regime.

records.title: Paso Canoas fiscal-protest and trucker blockade, September–October 2020
records.check_kind: Ledger reconciliation after two full source audits; not a new source-observation date
records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

Actual traffic resumed on 4 October 2020 before renewed obstruction that night, so September–October disruption is not one uninterrupted closure. The 4 October report describes several preceding suspended days but does not establish their exact onset. The renewed blockade is dated to the night of 4 October and documented again on 5 and 8 October; identical pedestrian effects throughout are not established. The government reported an agreement with one group on 12 October followed by occupation by others, without a measurable unrestricted gap. Its 14 October release contains inconsistent Wednesday/Thursday wording; dated Crítica reports establish barrier removal on 14 October and actual truck passage on 15 October. These later milestones are separate from a proven exact first reopening of every earlier phase. No additive or continuous fifteen-day duration is calculated.

Historical later-status finding retained where still applicable: Roadblocks removed October 14 and freight vehicles observed crossing October 15; use observed access, not the agreement alone.

phases.scope: Paso Canoas road before Panamanian customs

records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: qualified. Ten unnamed Houaphanh local posts closed March 13, 2020; later permission does not establish reopening of all ten.

R3-EA-008-FU1: Province-level reference only; exact gates and reopening unknown. Excludes separate national named-gate measures.

end/scope: No matching ten-post roster or reopening found.

duration: March 13 closure confirmation permits an onset observation only.

continuity: RFA's March 16 report quotes a March 13 Houaphanh notice and official confirmation that ten traditional/local posts closed while four international posts stayed open. Exact gate identities and later reopening remain unestablished.

By 2022-09-01, Laos had authorized provinces to reopen local and traditional border checkpoints under controls. This is later national permission, not proof of the reopening date or actual operation of all ten unnamed Houaphanh posts. No continuous closure through 2022 or beyond is established. Notification 1342/PMO dated 2020-12-10 also permits temporary necessary agricultural exports at Ban Dan–Xiengmouang, with dates still to be set. This is limited formal permission; the unnamed March roster does not establish that Ban Dan was one of the ten posts.

records.title: Austria suspends traffic on numerous designated minor frontier routes in March 2020
records.check_kind: Ledger reconciliation after two full source audits; not a new source-observation date
records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

The June 3 ministerial reply identifies separate closure orders dated March 13, March 17 and March 20, distinct from regulations merely introducing border checks. Contemporary APA reporting on March 13 places the 47 Italian-route suspensions at the following midnight; that is March 14, not the order’s publication date. The March 20 parliamentary account confirms the regime. Italian major crossings remained available, and Thörl-Maglern had reduced hours rather than full closure. The April and May amendments changed rosters, so no unchanged all-route interval is inferred. ORF’s May 17 police-attributed account establishes reopening of all Vorarlberg crossings, while pandemic admission conditions continued. It does not date reopening of other Austrian provinces. June 4 general admission easing is not substituted for a physical reopening of every minor route. Liechtenstein closures are separately recorded in R3-RT-001.

phases.scope: Designated fully suspended routes on Austria’s Swiss, German, Slovenian and Hungarian frontiers; Liechtenstein routes separately recorded.
47 designated minor routes on the Austria–Italy frontier, excluding retained major crossings and reduced-hour roads.

records.title: Lebanon–Syria COVID passenger closure regimes and phased exceptions, 2020–2021
records.check_kind: Ledger reconciliation after two full source audits; not a new source-observation date
records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

R3-ME-011-R1: Initial ordered window only. Primary Arabic resolves UNECE English midnight notation. Lebanon incoming land passengers only; Syrian-side rules, exits, actual reopening and later extensions are separate. Permitted return clause does not override preexisting Syria-country restriction.

R3-ME-011-C7P1: Continuation of the same initial passenger-arrival order, with UNIFIL, diplomatic, international-organization and Block 4-worker exceptions retained. April 12 is a scheduled last date; exact endpoint hour is not recovered. Not observed reopening and not Syrian-side operation.

R3-ME-011-C7P2: Dated status only; no onset or continuous link to the March–April orders inferred. Announced July 7 citizen return 09:00–16:00 is an exception, not a general passenger reopening.

Later partial access: Arabic reports dated March 18, 2021 reproduce General Security’s cohort-specific schedule at Masnaa and Abboudieh. This establishes a later policy easing observation; the one-sentence L’Orient newsflash alone does not establish completed throughput. Sources also describe medical, embassy-appointment and airport-transit exceptions at land posts. No continuous link from July 2020 or first physical reopening date is inferred.

December 13, 2021 is a later, nationality-specific Syrian entry easing supported by LBCI. It does not supply an endpoint for all Lebanese-side restrictions or prove uninterrupted closure between the earlier observations.

Historical later-status finding retained where still applicable: Current UNHCR guidance documents Masnaa/Qaa pedestrian and vehicle operation, and Arida/Boqayaa pedestrian operation. The former blanket passenger suspension has ended by the review date; this does not imply vehicle access at every crossing.

records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

R3-ME-013-REV1: Overlaps R3-ME-013-R1; do not add their durations. Special cargo and one-time stranded vehicles exempt. A separate May policy observation is recorded below, without assuming every February term remained unchanged.

Initial national decision: The February 6 issuance is reported by Enab Baladi on February 7, with a link to the authority’s notice. The original signed order and first enforcement at each gate have not been independently inspected. This observation neither backdates the February 13 bilateral terms nor proves continuous nationwide enforcement or later repeal.

May 9 observation: SANA’s May 10 report describes current transshipment measures and a Lebanese request for exemptions. The reported reactivation of the 1993 transport agreement is not an explicit repeal of these measures.

records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

R3-AF-002-D1: Contemporary AFP and April 2020 reporting support an October 11, 2019 closure and formal suspension through April 3, 2020, without proving universal uninterrupted enforcement. The reason for extending the independence-holiday closure remains unassigned.

A Cameroon Human Rights Commission report, page 20, quotes the Kye-Ossi immigration chief describing occasional openings for organised shopping groups in both directions from August 2022. Use the end of that month only as a conservative partial later-access bound, not an exact reopening date. The official describes the closure notification as October 12, 2019; this may be a notification/implementation distinction and does not displace the contemporary October 11 report.

The commission says formal reopening had not occurred at the time of its inquiry. GECAM’s March 2026 report describes continuing transit barriers, but does not establish every traveller or goods category. No uninterrupted 2019–2026 closure or full reopening is inferred.

Separately dated later evidence: 2022-08-31: Occasional organised shopping groups in both directions from August 2022; month-precision bound; formal repeal not established This evidence does not resolve the whole phase.

records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

R4-AM-005-D1: Excludes local work, study and medical exceptions that continued until July 1 tightening. This is not a total Macara closure or the endpoint for San Miguel/other Ecuador crossings; Rumichaca/Huaquillas remained authorised. Reopening time does not supply an exact onset hour.

R4-AM-005-AUDIT20261025-1: Lalamor is the crossing in Zapotillo canton, not an additional duplicate port. Ordinary vehicle traffic resumed on 8 July; pedestrian access had been separately restored by 4 July. San Miguel was still reported closed on 9 July, with controlled crude and special-permit exceptions. These dated observations do not establish October status.

R4-AM-005-R2P1–R2P3: Separate dated phases retain the closures at San Miguel, La Balsa and Jimbura rather than assigning them the Macará or Lalamor reopening. The Andean Community’s May order to withdraw the trade restriction is not evidence of restored operations. A later El Comercio article repeats San Miguel closure but its displayed dates change between retrievals; it is not used to advance the last-confirmed date. Neither the July observations nor that undated later account establishes status on October 26.

records.title: Latvia prohibits non-exempt passenger movement at Russian and Belarusian land borders in March 2020
records.check_kind: Ledger reconciliation after two full source audits; not a new source-observation date
records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: qualified. Fresh legal text and official indexed notices support the selected original phase and qualified 2021–2022 inward easing; no COVID extension into later sanctions.

Order 103 lost force June 10, 2020 and was replaced, rather than physically reopening all routes. Returnees, freight, transit and other exceptions persisted. Official guidance documents easing for certificate-qualified vaccinated/recovered entrants June 16, 2021 and removal of the significant-purpose entry requirement from March 1, 2022 regardless of country of entry; no specially high-risk countries were then listed. This is a latest inward policy bound, not proof that every original cohort was denied continuously until that day. Testing and certificates remained separate and were removed April 1 under the later March 29 decision. The full outward chronology, first actual passages and neighbouring-country restrictions remain unverified. Later Russia-related sanctions must not be labelled continuing COVID restrictions.

Scope reconciliation: The final audit limits the March 1 2022 policy-ending evidence to inward significant-purpose rules and explicitly leaves outward chronology incomplete. The native phase includes entry and exit, so that evidence does not resolve the whole phase.

phases.scope: Successor Latvian restrictions on non-exempt passenger movement at Russian and Belarusian land frontiers

This ended-by bound does not derive solely from the 1 October easing of personal travel. records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: qualified. Original February 24, 2022 onset and August 28, 2025 cohort change remain supported; later professional-exemption guidance is not a new general onset.

P1 began February 24, 2022 and ends only as a policy version on August 28, 2025, when the general 18–22 cohort exemption took effect. Resolution 1031 is the operative amendment; the district source’s 1030 reference is erroneous. This did not reopen travel for every male citizen or every crossing. P2 retains restrictions for non-exempt male citizens aged 23–60, with office-holder and other qualifications. April 1, 2026 official guidance confirms special permission procedures for male media professionals; September 29, 2026 reporting describes continuing older-cohort restrictions. These later observations do not reconstruct every exemption amendment or prove unchanged continuous operation. Mobilisation eligibility is distinct from permission to leave.

Historical later-status finding retained where still applicable: The general wartime exit restriction began on 24 February 2022 for non-exempt men aged 18–60. The 28 August 2025 exemption for men aged 18–22 narrowed the main age group to 23–60; that amendment must not appear as the original policy onset. Current guidance retains the non-exempt Ukrainian male-citizen exit restriction for ages 23–60; younger exemption and authorised exceptions remain.

records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

REC50-R17-004-P1 and P2: The specific official passenger suspension effective 15 February 2023, later checkpoint-specific reporting, and the March 2026 account of the reconstruction restriction establish real sustained restrictions above 24 hours. These scoped accounts take precedence over the December 2025 commissioning article’s broad statement that passenger and freight traffic was uninterrupted across the modernization programme. That broad statement remains a conflicting description, not a basis for erasing the documented passenger bans. Precise uninterrupted elapsed durations remain unquantified.

P1: Kazakh Atameken commissioning on 16 April 2025 did not restore paired personal passage while Uzbek bridge works continued. Actual personal and passenger-vehicle restoration at Uzbek Syrdarya is reported by 24 March 2026; the first day remains unknown.

P2: Kazygurt’s December 2025 commissioning does not independently establish first restored paired ordinary passenger passage. The November account describes construction starting in March 2023; the contemporaneous official measure specifies passenger suspension from 15 February 2023. Heavy freight continued, and no network-wide closure is asserted.

phases.scope: Kazygurt–S. Nadzhimov/Nazhimov ordinary persons, cars and buses under the shared reconstruction measure

records.title: Cristo Redentor truckers’ protest obstruction during COVID testing delays, January 2022
records.check_kind: Ledger reconciliation after two full source audits; not a new source-observation date
records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

The January 17 outbound obstruction is evidenced by physical blockage at the Uspallata control-area exit, not inferred from testing queues. The separate January 20 incoming-freight obstruction remains a later phase. January 25–26 reporting describes continuation and supports multi-day duration eligibility; minute-by-minute closure of every movement or one common bidirectional interval is not asserted. The La Nación clipping hosted by CERA also describes the incoming-truck blockade being maintained; its January 27 date is supplied by the clipping filename rather than a printed date in the article body.

The January 29 protocol change and January 30 general traffic-clearance report are distinct from a direction-matched first protest reopening. Radio Nacional’s January 31 participant-interview summary reports settlement, providing a later bound but not an exact operational endpoint. Its January 14 conflict date concerns the wider health-policy dispute, not the physical protest onset. A threatened customs-staff stoppage and separate tourist restrictions are excluded.

Historical later-status finding retained where still applicable: Radio Nacional interviewed a participating trucker on 31 January 2022 and reported that the Cristo Redentor protest had been settled following roughly fifteen days of disruption. A possible new customs-staff stoppage was a separate threat. This bounds the recorded January trucker blockade without extending it into later years.

phases.scope: Freight entering Argentina from Chile, deliberately obstructed by protesting truckers
Chile-bound freight leaving the Uspallata integrated-control area on the Argentine approach to Cristo Redentor

records.title: Ras Jedir trade and development protest campaign, December 2016–January 2017
records.check_kind: Ledger reconciliation after two full source audits; not a new source-observation date
records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: qualified. Two episodes remain necessary: December onset is distinct from January restoration and repeated openings rule out a continuous cross-month interval.

REC50-R21-002-P1: Emergency cases and Libyans returning home could pass. The two-week sit-in history is not the closure onset. Later repeated openings prevent extending this spell into January.

REC50-R21-002-P2: Ambulances and emergencies were exceptions. The 17 January deal did not itself restore traffic. The campaign included repeated openings; December-to-January continuity is not asserted.

phase boundaries and continuity: Two distinct scoped observations within one protest campaign: December blockage confirmed 13–14 December with unknown endpoint; January closure confirmed on 22 January and actual resumption on 23 January with unknown onset. No continuous cross-month duration.

Historical later-status finding retained where still applicable: Report explicitly describes traffic moving again after the Ben Guerdane protest; later April closure is separate.

phases.scope: Non-exempt passenger and goods passage at Ras Jedir crossing and Ben Guerdane approach

records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: qualified. The September 2023 temporary-entry prohibition is distinct from March 2024 requirements for cars already admitted; no reopening is supported.

The temporary-admission rule began September 16, 2023. Customs reported actual refusals and exempt admissions on both Russian and Norwegian frontiers by September 18. Its March 12, 2024 appendix confirms that the temporary-admission prohibition remains subject to exceptions. The March 15 removal deadline for previously admitted vehicles and March 16 documentation requirements are not reopening dates. Later physical road-post closures are separate. Fresh Finland-specific current confirmation and the full amendment chain after March 2024 remain unresolved; no uninterrupted refusal of all cars is asserted.

records.check_kind: Ledger reconciliation after two full source audits; not a new source-observation date
records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

REC50-R38-005-P1: Formal restoration is dated April 20, 2026. The inherited interruption is described approximately and as largely closed; exact onset, continuous exclusion and the original imposing order remain unknown. Contemporary April 20 Reuters soundbites still describe Rabia tanker exports prospectively. Rudaw on May 6 quotes deputy crossing director Basim Muhammad explicitly dating the first 70-tanker batch to May 1; SANA’s May 9 account separately repeats the Border Ports Authority’s May 1 announcement. This supplies a scoped operational date without asserting first passenger access or universal normal trade. UN humanitarian consignments crossed in March 2018–January 2020, so the inherited interruption cannot mean exclusion of all traffic. Carnegie research attributes blocked ordinary reopening to Baghdad’s position toward the Syrian authorities; it does not recover the original closure order.

REC50-R47-R38-005-P1: The January 16 UN briefing confirms that medical shipments had ceased. The Secretary-General’s February 21 report, using information through February 19, states that UN cross-border operations into the northeast no longer occurred following resolution 2504. This supports a multi-day service cessation and extends the evidence limit; the exact first missed shipment and matching restoration remain unknown. NGO operations and aid sent within Syria are different services. Neither April 2026 ordinary reopening nor May 1 tanker passage establishes restoration of this UN shipment mechanism.

records.finding:
Second full-register audit, 26 October 2026: additional source-audited corrections incorporated. See the phase, scope and qualification columns for the accepted findings.

P1–P3 retain the three completed March 29 actions. Contemporary reports describe Ruse and Kardam at nearly two hours and Vidin at approximately half an hour; these are reported durations, not exact independently logged clocks.

Later actions are now supported as occurrences: P4 and P5 on March 30, P6 at Kardam on March 31, and P7 at Durankulak on March 30 according to a named BTA interview on March 31. P4 has a same-day completion report. P5 and P6 lack a secure matched reopening; P7’s absence of protesters the next day does not give an exact first-passage time. These are discrete observations, not proof of continuous closure between dates.

P8–P9 are separate April 7 actions reported by BNR as completed after three hours, until 13:00; the substantive indexed BNR text was inspected, while its direct page returned an error. The April actions do not extend the March events. A screen of all current input readers found no duplicate phases on these dates. General protest schedules, planned April actions in older reports and Silistra port activity do not establish additional road-crossing intervals.

REC50-R47-003-P1: BGB-attributed land-admission denials are observed November 21 and December 1. This is a qualification of the admission regime, not an exact endpoint for the Ukhia/Ghumdhum land observations. The separately recorded UNHCR “urges open borders” webpage is dated 29 August 2017 and concerns a later displacement episode; it does not verify a 2016 reopening.

The September 16 primary notice announced application from September 17; the September 18 customs publication confirms the rule was in force. A Border Guard response obtained on September 18 reports one actual vehicle refusal, subsequently located on the Russian frontier in a PAP report. chronology_followup.method: Original separately sourced status observations and timelines retained unchanged, including their original check dates. Reconciliation does not extend their evidence dates.

historical_audit.method: All 221 records (250 last-confirmed phases) in the endpoint review inventory were researched on 25 October 2026. Findings distinguish current restrictions, later access bounds, changed scope, partial evidence, conflicting evidence and unresolved status. Selected map updates received source-text, date and scope checks; unavailable full text and inadequate evidence remain qualified. Standing official guidance is dated to the check; news observations retain their event/report date. A later access bound suppresses only the matching old unknown marker from that bound onward. It does not label the border open, alter historical durations, fill gaps or merge later reclosures. Status verification dates are not closure starts. Separately reviewed timeline periods show a restriction from its sourced effective date through its latest supporting evidence, with changing scopes, exceptions and reopenings separated. Pre-window regimes are labelled as already in force, not newly starting at the window boundary. Unreviewed snapshots, if any, remain confined to their evidence month. These supplemental periods are excluded from episode and duration statistics. Coverage concerns this fixed inventory, not every world frontier. A further COVID-focused pass separates the ending of a national prohibition from reopening every individual port. Each new resolution records whether it is based on policy cessation or later access; neither establishes present-day openness. The subsequent open-ended follow-up also records scope_changed bounds: the original blanket policy no longer applies as stated, but narrower conditions or security restrictions may persist. This is not a declaration of whole-border reopening.

audit.research_method: Record-by-record searches for later reopening, continuing restriction and current guidance; government, border agency, customs, UN and direct operational reporting preferred. Scope checked by crossing, movement, direction, cohort and commodity. Plans, expired orders, fresh crawl dates, opposite-direction movement and unrelated ports were not treated as reopenings. Sources shown include both adopted evidence and rejected or insufficient leads as explained in each finding. Search-result extracts were used where direct retrieval failed; this is a source review, not field verification or independent human review.

covid_followup.method: Follow-up prioritised pandemic restrictions still appearing as unknown in 2025. National policy phases are matched to policy cessation; operational phases require evidence of the affected movement at the named crossing. Testing alone does not prolong an admission ban. Partial reopening is not applied to unmatched crossings. No automatic pandemic cutoff or inferred continuing closure is introduced.

chronology_followup.method: Each status observation was checked against its prior chronology and source evidence. Effective dates, pre-window regimes, changes of legal scope and genuine reclosures are separate from observation/check dates. Continuity describes the stated access regime with exceptions, not a measured daily closure duration. Source-access limits remain visible in the underlying record and the observation notes.

open_ended_followup.method: Follow-up checks distinguish exact policy changes, observed resumption, later-access bounds and continuing named-post restrictions. A changed blanket policy can stop the old broad marker without establishing unrestricted entry at every port. Dated event text takes precedence over page mastheads; plans and announced expiry dates are not observed reopenings. No global pandemic cutoff is used. Continuing restrictions are dated from their effective date, not this review date; no whole-frontier geometry is substituted for unlocated named posts.
